facts.text: Stability is a machine's resistance to tipping, sliding or losing control.

facts.text: Hard braking is itself a hazard because it throws the load forward and can push a machine past its limits.

facts.text: Braking near a dump edge loads ground that is already marginal.

facts.text: Hazards from an automatic stop include rollover or unloading instability, articulation and yaw instability, loss of directional control or runaway on grade or loose ground, payload movement or spill, sliding or ground failure near edges, operator injury from sudden stops, secondary collisions, and rollaway after the intervention.
facts.quote: rollover or unloading instability, articulation and yaw instability, loss of directional control or runaway on grade or loose ground, payload movement or spill, sliding or ground failure near edges, operator injury from sudden stops, secondary collisions, and rollaway after the intervention

facts.text: Underground workers describe automatic stops as "jarring and jolting."
facts.quote: Underground workers describe "jarring and jolting" stops

facts.text: Mine leaders preferred systems that first slow to a crawl and only then set the brake.

facts.text: One wheel loader manufacturer's documentation tells users to switch the stop function off on steep slopes, on slippery or soft ground and with suspended loads.

facts.text: The automatic brake must command the smallest deceleration that avoids the collision, limited by traction, stability, brake capability and the load.

facts.text: Safe deceleration limits must be derived per machine family, with stability tests in the physical campaign covering braking with steering or articulation, on cross-slope, and at relevant payloads.
